outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the imagery, narrative, and dark tone of the original while refining the language and rhythm:

---

They carried my body into the forest,
bid me climb a ladder.
I did not wish to climb,
yet they forced me upward still.

*If you refuse the ladder,
we will bury you in the foaming mud.*

So I was left to choose:
death by the noose, or death by earth.

I climbed, and they fastened
a belt around the tree's broad limb.
And when at last my breath gave out,
they cast me into the stream below.

I drifted to the village's edge,
where someone whispered a prayer for my soul.

This is how it goes,
in a lullaby for the world's ending—
the paths to that final silence
are without number.

But this is not truly such a lullaby.
It speaks instead of beginnings—
of what unfolds when we begin to rot
beneath the open sky,
how the light falls upon
the ants, the worms, the parasites
that feast upon our flesh.

It speaks of packs of dogs
gnawing at skin and bone.

Do you know the sensation
of a ghost's tongue upon your entrails?
Do you know what it means
for a rat to consume your mind?

To escape the pit,
the children must sing gently, softly.
To escape the pit,
their songs must overflow with love.

# The Lullaby That Isn't

They took me to the forest when the light had gone thin and gray, the trees standing like witnesses who would never speak. I remember the ladder most of all—how my hands shook against the rough wood, how the voice behind me made it clear there was no going back down. Climb, they said, or the mud waits below, patient and dark, ready to swallow you whole and hold you there until your lungs forgot what air was for.

So I climbed.

At the top, they gave me a choice, though it was hardly a choice at all: the earth or the rope. Drown slowly in the wet black ground, or hang from the limb until breath became a memory. I chose the tree. I chose the branch and the rough fiber biting into my neck, chose the long moment where my feet searched for ground that wasn't there, chose the burning in my chest that dulled into something quieter, something final.

When it was over, they didn't bury me. They didn't need to. They rolled me into the stream instead, and the water carried me the way water carries anything that no longer struggles—gently, indifferently, downstream toward a village I would never see with living eyes. Someone there, a stranger perhaps, or someone who somehow knew, knelt at the bank and said a prayer for whatever remained of me. A small mercy. A soul, if that's what it was, given a moment's acknowledgment before the world moved on.

Now, let me tell you what this song is really about, because the title has misled you. This is not a lullaby for the end of the world, not some grand ballad of apocalypse and cosmic silence. No—this is smaller and closer than that. This is a song about beginnings. About the beginning of what happens after: the flies that find you first, patient and thorough; the small crawling things that make a home of what you no longer need; the dogs that come sniffing at the edges of things, drawn by what the wind carries. This is a song about decay in its earliest hours, about the body becoming something else entirely, piece by piece, in vivid, unflinching detail.

So here is what I tell the children, the ones who still have breath to spare and choices left to make:

Sing softly. Sing sweetly. Let every note you offer the night be gentle, be full of love, be careful and kind. Because the alternative is the hole, the rope, the stream, the flies. The alternative is becoming a lesson passed down through a song that pretends to be about endings but is really about all the small, terrible beginnings that follow.

Sing sweetly, children. Sing soft.

The forest is listening.
outputs.L4:
# The Ladder

They told me: climb.
The rungs were wet with something
I did not want to name, and my hands
remembered how to grip
even as my mind refused.

Above, a rope. Below,
a pit already dug, the earth
turned back like a lip peeled from teeth.
*Choose*, they said, though it was no choice—
the noose or the dirt,
the quick drop or the long dark,
breath stolen fast or stolen slow.

I climbed because the body climbs
even when the soul has already
lain down in surrender.
Each rung took me closer to the sky
that would not save me,
closer to the branch
that held the weight of every name
before mine.

*

This is not a song to close your eyes to.
Not the hush of *sleep now, sleep now*
that mothers hum when day is done.
No—this is what comes after singing stops,
after the last breath leaves
and the body becomes
a stranger to itself.

I have seen how quickly
the sweetness drains from flesh,
how fast the vessel that held laughter
becomes only vessel,
becomes matter,
becomes food for smaller mouths
that do not know they feast on what was once
someone's whole and beating world.

The skin forgets its warmth first.
Then the color leaves, slow as dusk
but with none of dusk's mercy.
What is left is not the end—
it is only the beginning
of a different kind of becoming,
the grotesque architecture
of what we are when we are
no longer *who* we are.

*

So climb the ladder if you must.
Choose the rope or choose the pit.
But children—listen—

this is why you must sing.

Not the songs that promise rest,
not lullabies that mean *the end*,
but songs stitched from sweetness,
from love that refuses
to become mere matter,
refuses the grotesque unbecoming
that waits at the bottom
of every silence.

Sing loud enough to fill the space
before the rope, before the pit.
Sing so the sweetness in your throat
becomes armor, becomes light,
becomes the thing that decay
cannot touch, cannot claim,
cannot turn to dirt.

For the world may end in many ways—
but you, small singers,
you can choose to leave it
not as strangers to your flesh
but as voices still ringing,
still climbing toward something
that is not the ladder,
not the noose,
not the grave—

but the sound of love
outlasting every ending
we were ever told
we had to choose.
outputs.L5:
# They, The

They arrived at dusk, when the sky wore its deepest orange and the streets had emptied of their usual noise. The town had heard rumors—whispers passed from porch to porch—but nothing prepares a place for the reality of change.

They did not announce themselves. They simply were, standing at the edge of the old market square as though they had always belonged there. The children noticed first, as children often do. They pointed, tugged at sleeves, asked questions that adults struggled to answer.

The days that followed unfolded slowly. They walked through the town without hurry, observing the shops, the gardens, the small rituals of daily life. The townspeople watched in return, uncertain whether to feel fear or curiosity. They seemed to expect neither.

What they wanted remained unclear for weeks. The mayor called meetings. The council debated. Yet through it all, they simply continued their quiet presence, as if patience itself were their only language.

Eventually, the truth emerged—not through grand revelation, but through small gestures. They helped an old farmer repair his fence. They sat with the lonely widow on her porch, saying nothing, offering only company. The town began to understand that they had not come to take, but perhaps only to witness, to learn, to be near.

By the time autumn arrived, the line between "they" and "we" had blurred into something softer. The strangers had become neighbors. The unfamiliar had become simply *known*.

And in the end, that was the story worth telling: not of arrival or departure, but of the space between—the slow, uncertain bridge that they and the town built together, one quiet day at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal poem about death by hanging that reads like a twisted lullaby, with vivid imagery of decay and nature reclaiming the body.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rope-Swing Lullaby

Hush now, darling, don't you cry,
the tree has made a friend tonight—
a shadow-shape that swings so slow,
its toes just kissing shadows below.

Hush-a-bye, the branches creak,
a wooden mother's lullaby speak,
rock-a-bye upon the bough,
the wind will braid your hair for now.

The crows have come to count your teeth,
they take them one by one beneath
a moon that watches, pale and round,
too polite to make a sound.

Sleep, sleep, your fingers curl
like question marks around the world,
and ivy climbs your ankle bone,
mistaking you for something grown.

The beetles write their names in you,
in cursive dark and morning-dew,
and mushrooms bloom where your breath once was—
soft little moons, without a cause.

Hush now, hush, the night is old,
your skin has turned to something gold
and green and brown and finally earth,
a slow unmaking, a backwards birth.

The tree don't mind the weight you give,
it's learned new ways for you to live—
in root and rot and rising sap,
in every leaf's small, silent clap.

So rock-a-bye, don't make a peep,
the forest keeps what it will keep,
and you're not gone, not gone, my dear—
just scattered soft through atmosphere.

Hush now, darling, don't you cry,
we all get borrowed by the sky,
and what was rope is now a vine,
and what was you is oak, and pine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a free-verse poem in the voice of a ghost describing their own execution and decomposition, using unsettling and grotesque imagery?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rope Remembers

I keep the date in my throat now—
a knot the weather never loosens.

They walked me up the wooden stairs
counting each one like a rosary
made of teeth. Someone coughed.
Someone always coughs at hangings,
as if the body needs to prove
it's still afraid of dying.

The bag they placed over my face
smelled of other men's last breaths,
sour wheat and fear-sweat,
a communion I didn't ask to take.

Then the floor forgot me.

I remember the sound most—
not a snap, no mercy in it,
just a long wet argument
between my neck and gravity,
settled badly, settled slow.

*

They cut me down by Tuesday.
The crows had already started
their inventory—
soft tissue first, always,
the eyes going like grapes
plucked by patient fingers,
the cheeks caving in
like a house giving up its roof.

I watched from somewhere close
and elsewhere, the way you watch
a movie about a stranger
who happens to wear your face.

My tongue, swollen violet,
protruded like a slug
tasting the last of the air.
The maggots came in April—
white, industrious, devout,
turning my stomach into lace,
into a wet cathedral
where something small could worship.

*

Skin is the first liar to leave.
It slides off like a coat
someone else needed more.
Then the smell—
sweet the way rot is sweet,
like fruit that forgot
it was supposed to nourish
instead of announce.

My hands, still cuffed,
became two calcium apologies,
fingers curling inward
as if reaching for a door
that had already
closed.

*

Now I am mostly architecture—
a scaffold of what I was,
ribs like the hull
of a ship that never learned to float,
skull cradling rainwater,
a little moon in a little bowl
of bone.

The grass grew through my sternum
in June. I didn't mind.
Something had to.

*

I don't haunt the gallows out of anger.
I haunt it because this is where
I last had a shape
worth remembering,
where the rope and I
agreed, finally,
on gravity,

on silence,

on the long, unglamorous work
of coming apart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a disturbing "lullaby for the end of the world" poem that starts with violence and forced death, then shifts into imagery of rot, insects, and scavenging animals.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lullaby for the Last Night

Hush now, darling, don't you cry,
the blade is quick, you'll barely die—
a whisper-cut across the throat,
a crimson ribbon, a final note.

Sleep now, sleep, the choir sings sweet
while ash rains soft on empty streets.
The gunshots echo, then go still,
the world grows quiet, as it will.

Hush now, hush, the fire's warm,
it wraps you like a mother's arm.
No need to run, no need to fight—
just close your eyes and lose the light.

*

Now let the maggots write their psalm
across your flesh, so white, so calm.
They know a lullaby of their own,
a slow sweet hymn of flesh from bone.

The beetles come in black processions,
carrying away your last confessions.
The flies compose their humming choir,
singing praises to the pyre.

Sleep now, sleep, the crows convene,
they've never seen a feast so clean.
They pick your ribs like silver strings,
and something almost like song, it sings.

The foxes come when moonlight's thin,
to nose the place your soul had been.
They do not mourn, they do not weep—
they simply help the earth to sleep.

Hush now, hush, the world unmakes
itself in slow, deliberate flakes.
The soil drinks what you become,
and hums you back where you're from.

Sleep now, sleep, there's no more pain,
just rot, and root, and gentle rain.
The insects hum, the scavengers sigh—
this is how the whole world says goodbye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic narrative told in first person about being forced to choose between hanging and burial, followed by a meditation on bodily decay and what children must do to escape a similar fate.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Choosing

They gave me this: a rope or earth,
as if mercy wore two faces
and I should thank them for the pair.

I have thought on it too long now,
turning the choice like a coin
that shows the same dark metal
on either side.

The rope would have me dance
a moment's dance, my body
the clapper in some terrible bell,
and then—the long hang after,
crows finding what the crowd forgets,
my feet pointing at nothing,
at everyone.

The earth is patient. The earth
has always been patient with us,
taking soldiers and infants
with the same slow mouth.
No ceremony in the ground,
just the weight of it,
just the dark doing what dark does—
unstitching me, thread by thread,
until I am only
what the worms didn't want,
until I am the taste
that makes grass greener
in one particular corner
of one particular field.

*

This is what happens after, if you want to know:
the water in us goes first, sweated back
to whatever cloud we borrowed it from.
Then the soft architecture—
what let us laugh, what let us weep,
what made the sound of our name
in our own mouths—all of it
surrenders to the small mouths
that have no names to lose.

Bone holds out longest,
stubborn as memory,
white flag we never meant to wave
but wave regardless, wave for years,
until even bone relents
and rain finds a way to argue
calcium back into rivers,
into fish, into the birds
that eat the fish,
into a child, perhaps,
drinking from a stream
not knowing she drinks
the patience of the dead.

*

So here is what I'd tell the children,
if children ever listened to the dead
before becoming dead themselves:

Run. Not from this body's ending—
that argument was settled
before you were born,
written in whatever made you
in the first place.

Run from the smallness of it.
Run from rooms where choices
narrow to a rope or a hole.
Run toward wideness,
toward horizons that don't ask you
to pick your own erasure.

Because the body decays regardless—
this is not the tragedy.
The tragedy is choosing
between two kinds of forgetting
when you might have lived
so loudly, so widely,
that forgetting had to work
a little harder
to find you.

Go now. Go far.
Let the rope and the earth
wait for someone else's choosing.
Let your own dance
be the one you pick,
in daylight,
on your own two feet,
before any of this
is asked of you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
